new_statements.quote: [p.89] Chadic languages make use of three prosodic properties: tone, intonation, and syllable weight. All Chadic languages are tone languages, i.e. relative voice pitch on individual syllables is part of the lexical representation of words and has the potential for making morphosyntactic distinctions. [...] Stress as distinctive prosodic property has been discussed in Hunter (1980) for Hausa and Wolff (1983, 2015b) for Lamang (and perhaps in a few other Chadic language studies), but prosodic amplitude in Chadic phonological systems generally is a function of the interaction of tone, syllable weight, and intonation and plays no role that is not attributable to those properties. [p.6] - stress: no Chadic language has stress as a prosodic parameter

new_statements.rule_in_words: Per Schuh (who himself produced the only phonological sketch of Galambu, 1978), every Chadic language, hence Galambu, is a lexical/grammatical tone language and none has word stress as an independent prosodic parameter; perceived prominence follows from tone, syllable weight and intonation.
new_statements.exceptions: Schuh notes that stress 'as distinctive prosodic property' has been argued for Hausa (Hunter 1980) and Lamang (Wolff 1983, 2015b) but rejects an independent role for it; no Bole-Tangale exceptions named.
new_statements.domain_note: FAMILY-LEVEL generalization over all Chadic languages, not a Galambu-specific description; Galambu is only named in the book's Bole-Tangale language list. The Galambu-specific phonological sketch is in Schuh 1978 (print only, not seen). Word-level prosody; no discussion of citation forms or phrase-level prominence for Galambu.
new_statements.identity_note: The quoted statement is a family-level generalization over all Chadic languages by R. G. Schuh (A Chadic Cornucopia, 2017), not a description of Galambu (gala1264) itself; Schuh is also the author of the only Galambu-specific phonological sketch (1978, print only, not seen). Decker et al. 2022 call the language Galambi and sampled the Pada and Yelwa varieties. If the catalog requires a language-specific statement, treat this entry as provisional pending Schuh 1978.
